tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. <result># Investigation Report: rbtree-lab fuzzer

## 1. `include/rbtree.h` — full contents (the graded, immutable contract)

```c
#ifndef RBTREE_H
#define RBTREE_H
#include <stddef.h>
typedef struct rbtree rbtree_t;
typedef void (*rb_value_free_fn)(void *value);
/* Returns NULL on allocation failure.
* value_free may be NULL (values not owned). */
rbtree_t *rb_create(rb_value_free_fn value_free);
/* Copies key (tree owns the copy).
* Takes ownership of value ONLY on success.
* Overwriting an existing key frees the old value via value_free.
* Returns 0 on success, -1 on allocation failure (tree unchanged, value NOT
* consumed; caller still owns it). */
int rb_insert(rbtree_t *t, const char *key, void *value);
/* Returns the value, or NULL if absent. Tree retains ownership. */
void *rb_find(const rbtree_t *t, const char *key);
/* Removes key; frees the key copy and the value.
* Returns 0, or -1 if absent. */
int rb_delete(rbtree_t *t, const char *key);
size_t rb_size(const rbtree_t *t);
/* In-order traversal. */
void rb_foreach(const rbtree_t *t,
                void (*fn)(const char *key, void *value, void *ctx),
                void *ctx);
/* Returns 0 iff all red-black invariants hold
* (see the baseline section). */
int rb_validate(const rbtree_t *t);
/* Frees all nodes, key copies, and (if owned) values. NULL-safe. */
void rb_destroy(rbtree_t *t);
#endif
```

Key contract points:
- Keys are C strings (`const char *`); the tree copies them internally (`dup_key` in rbtree.c uses malloc/memcpy, not strdup — deliberately, to stay clean under `-std=c23 -Werror`).
- `rb_insert` returns **0/-1**, not errno-style codes. -1 only on allocation failure or NULL `t`/`key`; on failure the tree is unchanged and the caller-supplied `value` is *not* consumed (caller must still free it).
- `rb_delete` returns 0 on success, -1 if key absent or `t`/`key` NULL.
- `rb_find` returns NULL both for "absent" and (implicitly) can't distinguish from a legitimately-NULL-valued entry — note tests do store NULL values deliberately (see below) and rely on `rb_size`/`rb_validate`, not `rb_find`, to prove presence in that case.
- `rb_size` and `rb_validate` are both NULL-safe (`rb_size(NULL) == 0`, `rb_validate(NULL) == -1`).
- `rb_destroy` is NULL-safe.
- `rb_validate` returns 0 iff all RB invariants hold (root black, no red-red, equal black-heights, strictly increasing in-order keys, and size matches node count — see rbtree.c internals below).
- CLAUDE.md hard constraint: **rbtree.h must never be modified** — it's the graded contract, so a fuzzer must work purely against this API.

## 2. `tests/fuzz.c` — already exists, full current contents

Yes, it already exists (76 lines). Full text reproduced above in the tool output; summary of what it does:
- `main(argc, argv)`: `argv[1]` = iteration count (default 1000).
- Creates one tree with `rb_create(free)` (owning).
- Custom xorshift-style LCG seeded with a **fixed constant** `2463534242u`, updated as `lcg = lcg * 1103515245u + 12345u` (same constants test_rbtree.c uses) — deterministic, no `srand`/`rand`.
- Bounded keyspace of 200 keys (`k000`..`k199`) via `mkkey`/`KEYSPACE`.
- Each iteration picks op ∈ {insert, find, delete} (mod 3) and a key index (mod KEYSPACE) derived from different bit-shifts of the same LCG word.
- Insert: mallocs a 1-byte value, checks OOM, calls `rb_insert`; on failure frees the value and aborts (since tree didn't consume it) — correctly honoring the ownership contract.
- Delete: ignores -1 (miss) as expected/fine.
- Calls `rb_validate` every 50 iterations (not every iteration, to bound cost) and once more at the end.
- After the main loop, runs 1000 extra plain `rb_create(NULL)`/`rb_destroy` cycles ("allocation-path coverage").
- On success prints a one-line summary and returns `EXIT_SUCCESS`.
- No malloc-failure injection/fault injection, no reference-model cross-check against a shadow structure (it only trusts `rb_validate` + size), no CLI/env-based seed override, no multiple independent trees, no `rb_foreach` exercise, no explicit `rb_find` correctness check against expected membership (result of find is discarded), and note there's a leftover `vgcore.3345800` core dump (20 MB) sitting in the repo root — worth asking whether that's a crash from a prior fuzz/memcheck run that should be investigated (i.e., there may be a live bug) or just cleaned up. I did not open it (binary core dump), but its presence alongside `make memcheck` running `./$(FUZZBIN) 20000` suggests the fuzzer or memcheck run crashed at some point.

## 3. `Makefile` — full contents

```makefile
CC := gcc
CFLAGS := -std=c23 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -g -O1 -Iinclude
SRC := src/rbtree.c
TSRC := tests/test_rbtree.c
BIN := build/test_rbtree
FUZZBIN := build/fuzz
all: $(BIN) $(FUZZBIN)
$(BIN): $(SRC) $(TSRC) include/rbtree.h
	@mkdir -p build
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) $(SRC) $(TSRC) -o $@
$(FUZZBIN): $(SRC) tests/fuzz.c include/rbtree.h
	@mkdir -p build
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) $(SRC) tests/fuzz.c -o $@
test: $(BIN) $(FUZZBIN)
	./$(BIN) && ./$(FUZZBIN) 100000
asan: CFLAGS += -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer
asan: clean test
memcheck: all
	valgrind --leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=all \
		--error-exitcode=1 ./$(BIN)
	valgrind --leak-check=full --show-leak-kinds=all \
		--error-exitcode=1 ./$(FUZZBIN) 20000
clean:
	rm -rf build
.PHONY: all test asan memcheck clean
```

Notes:
- `fuzz.c` is **already fully wired in**: `all` builds both binaries, `test` runs `test_rbtree` then `fuzz 100000`, `asan` rebuilds everything (including fuzz) with `-fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer` added to CFLAGS then runs `test`, and `memcheck` runs valgrind on both binaries (`fuzz 20000` for the fuzz binary).
- Compiler: gcc, `-std=c23 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -g -O1 -Iinclude`. No `-fsanitize=fuzzer` (libFuzzer) target — this is a standalone/"dumb" harness driven by an iteration count, not a libFuzzer-style `LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput` corpus fuzzer.
- Both `$(BIN)` and `$(FUZZBIN)` depend on `include/rbtree.h`, `src/rbtree.c`, and their respective driver — any change to fuzz.c triggers a rebuild automatically.
- `build/` already contains compiled `test_rbtree` and `fuzz` binaries from a previous run.

## 4. `tests/test_rbtree.c` — reusable patterns (488 lines, skimmed in full)

- **Linking**: compiled directly against `src/rbtree.c` + `include/rbtree.h` (whitebox at build level, but only calls the public API — no internal struct access).
- **`CHECK(cond)` macro**: prints `FAIL file:line: cond` to stderr and increments a global `failures` counter; `main` returns `EXIT_SUCCESS` iff `failures == 0`. A fuzzer could reuse this macro/pattern for consistency, or keep its own simpler abort-on-first-failure style like fuzz.c currently does.
- **`heap_val()`**: helper returning a 1-byte malloc'd pointer, aborting the test on OOM — same idea fuzz.c uses inline.
- **`counting_free`**: a `value_free` wrapper that also increments a global `value_frees` counter — a simple way to independently verify ownership/frees happened the right number of times. Fuzz.c doesn't currently use anything like this (it just uses plain `free`), so this is a good pattern to borrow for detecting leaks/double-frees logically rather than relying only on valgrind/ASan.
- **`mkkey(buf, bufsz, i)`**: identical helper duplicated in both test_rbtree.c and fuzz.c — formats `k%03d` into a caller buffer (≥5 bytes, size 16 used).
- **No separate reference-model (shadow array/list) structure exists** — tests instead rely on: rb_validate() after most mutations, rb_size() equality checks, explicit rb_find() equality checks against expected pointer values, and a `char seen[N]`/`char done[N]` boolean array purely to track *which keys have been inserted/deleted so far* (not a full shadow key/value store). This `seen[]` boolean-array-tracking-visited-keys pattern is the closest thing to a reference model here, and would need to be extended (e.g., to a `void *shadow[KEYSPACE]` array) for a fuzzer that wants to cross-check `rb_find` results and detect logic bugs beyond invariant violations.
- **PRNG / shuffle pattern**: `unsigned int lcg = <fixed seed>; lcg = lcg * 1103515245u + 12345u;` then `(lcg >> 16) % N` for an index — this exact LCG (classic glibc-style constants) is used four separate times in test_rbtree.c with different fixed seeds (12345u, 987654321u, 555555555u) and is exactly what fuzz.c also uses (seed 2463534242u). This is the established repo-wide convention — see item 6 below.
- **rb_validate usage**: called after essentially every insert/delete in the "ascending", "descending", "shuffled insert", and "shuffled insert+delete" sections — i.e., validate after every single mutation is the norm in the unit tests (affordable there because N ≤ 150), whereas fuzz.c intentionally validates only every 50 iterations plus at the end because it runs up to 100k iterations and rb_validate is O(n).
- **Malloc-failure checking convention**: `heap_val()` checks its own malloc for NULL and calls `exit(EXIT_FAILURE)` on OOM (it doesn't try to test rb_insert's OOM path); there is no fault-injection/malloc-interposition test of `rb_insert`'s -1-return path in test_rbtree.c — that contract is exercised only indirectly by argument-validation checks (`rb_insert(t, NULL, nv) == -1`). No existing pattern for simulating real allocator OOM to hit `rb_insert`'s `goto fail`/`goto fail_node` paths.
- **Ownership/ordering checks**: extensive checks that `value_free` (i) is called exactly once per removed/overwritten/destroyed value, (ii) is never called with NULL when the stored value was NULL (guarded in rbtree.c), and (iii) leaves non-owned values untouched — all directly relevant if a fuzzer wants to add its own leak/double-free accounting layer.
- **rb_foreach usage**: verified for in-order-ness, visit count vs `rb_size`, and a running sum checksum via a small `foreach_ctx_t` struct + `foreach_visit` callback — fuzz.c currently never calls `rb_foreach` at all, which is a coverage gap.
- Style conventions: invariant comments on every "non-obvious" loop (per CLAUDE.md), `(void *)(intptr_t)i` used to stash small integers as opaque values when the tree is non-owning, `snprintf`-based key formatting into stack buffers of size 16.

## 5. `src/rbtree.c` — internals relevant to fuzzing

- **Node struct** (`rb_node_t`, private to the .c file — not visible to fuzz.c since it only includes rbtree.h):
```c
typedef struct rb_node {
    char *key;
    void *value;
    rb_color_t color;   /* enum { RED, BLACK } */
    struct rb_node *parent, *left, *right;
} rb_node_t;
```
- **`struct rbtree`** (opaque): `root`, a shared sentinel `nil` (always BLACK, self-referential), `value_free`, and `size` (size_t, maintained incrementally, O(1) `rb_size`).
- **Error/return codes**: `rb_create` returns NULL on OOM (frees any partial allocation first). `rb_insert` returns 0/-1: -1 for NULL `t`/`key`, or if either the node malloc (`malloc(sizeof *n)`) or key-copy malloc (in `dup_key`) fails — tree left completely unchanged on any -1, and `value` is never freed/consumed by the tree in that case (caller retains ownership). `rb_delete` returns 0/-1: -1 for NULL `t`/`key` or key-not-found; no allocation happens in delete so -1 there is never an OOM case. `rb_validate` returns 0/-1 (not a count or bitmask).
- **`rb_validate`/`rb_check`** internals check, in order: root is BLACK (property 1); no red node has a red child (property 2, nil reads as BLACK); in-order keys strictly increasing via `strcmp` (property 4, BST property); equal black-heights on both sides of every node (property 3); and finally that the walked node count equals the cached `t->size` (property 5) — this last check means a fuzzer's own external node-count tracking should exactly match `rb_size()`, and any drift is already caught by `rb_validate` itself.
- **Size/count function**: `size_t rb_size(const rbtree_t *t)` — O(1), NULL-safe (returns 0). No separate node-count-walk function is exposed publicly (the internal walk lives only inside `rb_check`, static).
- No `rb_min`/`rb_max`/iterator/cursor API beyond `rb_foreach` — a fuzzer wanting sorted-order snapshots must use `rb_foreach` into a caller-owned buffer/array.
- `dup_key` deliberately avoids `strdup` (may not be declared under strict C23 glibc headers, which would trip `-Werror`) — relevant if the fuzzer harness needs its own string duplication helper, avoid `strdup` too for consistency, or explicitly guard it.

## 6. Randomness/PRNG conventions repo-wide

- **No `rand()`/`srand()` used anywhere** in test_rbtree.c or fuzz.c.
- Convention is a **custom, fully deterministic 32-bit LCG**, always seeded with a **fixed integer literal** (never time-based), of the form:
  ```c
  unsigned int lcg = <fixed seed>;
  lcg = lcg * 1103515245u + 12345u;
  int idx = (int)((lcg >> 16) % N);
  ```
  These are the classic glibc `rand()` LCG constants (multiplier `1103515245`, increment `12345`), reimplemented by hand rather than calling libc's RNG — likely to keep results 100% reproducible across platforms/libc versions and independent of any `srand` call elsewhere in the process.
- Different fixed seeds are used per test section (e.g., `12345u`, `987654321u`, `246813579u`, `555555555u` in test_rbtree.c; `2463534242u` in fuzz.c), and different bit-shifts/moduli of the same generator are reused for op-selection vs. index-selection in fuzz.c (`lcg >> 16` for index, `lcg >> 8` for op) — i.e., squeezing multiple "random" fields out of one 32-bit LCG word rather than calling it multiple times per iteration.
- No existing use of `arc4random`, `/dev/urandom`, `getrandom()`, or any seed-from-argv/seed-from-env mechanism — reproducibility is achieved purely via hardcoded seeds, so if the upgraded fuzzer wants a CLI-overridable seed (common ask for fuzzers), that would be a new pattern, not an existing one to mimic.

## Other relevant observations
- `/s/chopin/n/under/C836889845/CS370/rbtree-lab/vgcore.3345800` — a 20 MB core dump sitting in the repo root, dated the same day as the last edits to `tests/fuzz.c`. This strongly suggests a crash occurred during a `make memcheck` (valgrind) or manual run of the fuzz binary. ## 1. `include/rbtree.h` — full contents (the graded, immutable contract)

```c
#ifndef RBTREE_H
#define RBTREE_H
#include <stddef.h>
typedef struct rbtree rbtree_t;
typedef void (*rb_value_free_fn)(void *value);
/* Returns NULL on allocation failure.
* value_free may be NULL (values not owned). */
rbtree_t *rb_create(rb_value_free_fn value_free);
/* Copies key (tree owns the copy).
* Takes ownership of value ONLY on success.
* Overwriting an existing key frees the old value via value_free.
* Returns 0 on success, -1 on allocation failure (tree unchanged, value NOT
* consumed; caller still owns it). */
int rb_insert(rbtree_t *t, const char *key, void *value);
/* Returns the value, or NULL if absent. Tree retains ownership. */
void *rb_find(const rbtree_t *t, const char *key);
/* Removes key; frees the key copy and the value.
* Returns 0, or -1 if absent. */
int rb_delete(rbtree_t *t, const char *key);
size_t rb_size(const rbtree_t *t);
/* In-order traversal. */
void rb_foreach(const rbtree_t *t,
                void (*fn)(const char *key, void *value, void *ctx),
                void *ctx);
/* Returns 0 iff all red-black invariants hold
* (see the baseline section). */
int rb_validate(const rbtree_t *t);
/* Frees all nodes, key copies, and (if owned) values. NULL-safe. */
void rb_destroy(rbtree_t *t);
#endif
```

Key contract points:
- Keys are C strings (`const char *`); the tree copies them internally (`dup_key` in rbtree.c uses malloc/memcpy, not strdup — deliberately, to stay clean under `-std=c23 -Werror`).
- `rb_insert` returns **0/-1**, not errno-style codes. -1 only on allocation failure or NULL `t`/`key`; on failure the tree is unchanged and the caller-supplied `value` is *not* consumed (caller must still free it).
- `rb_delete` returns 0 on success, -1 if key absent or `t`/`key` NULL.
- `rb_find` returns NULL both for "absent" and (implicitly) can't distinguish from a legitimately-NULL-valued entry — note tests do store NULL values deliberately (see below) and rely on `rb_size`/`rb_validate`, not `rb_find`, to prove presence in that case.
- `rb_size` and `rb_validate` are both NULL-safe (`rb_size(NULL) == 0`, `rb_validate(NULL) == -1`).
- `rb_destroy` is NULL-safe.
- `rb_validate` returns 0 iff all RB invariants hold (root black, no red-red, equal black-heights, strictly increasing in-order keys, and size matches node count — see rbtree.c internals below).

typedef struct rb_node {
    char *key;
    void *value;
    rb_color_t color;   /* enum { RED, BLACK } */

# Upgrade tests/fuzz.c: reference-model cross-checking

## Context

`tests/fuzz.c` already exists and is wired into the Makefile (`make test` runs it
with 100000 iterations; `make memcheck` with 20000 under valgrind; `make asan`
rebuilds everything with ASan/UBSan and reruns `make test`). It drives a
deterministic LCG-seeded mix of insert/find/delete against one tree over a
bounded 200-key keyspace, and periodically calls `rb_validate` — but only every
50 iterations, and it **only checks structural RB invariants** (balance,
ordering, size-matches-node-count). It never cross-checks that `rb_find`
returns the *correct* value or that `rb_delete`'s hit/miss return code is
*correct* — a logic bug that happens to preserve RB invariants (e.g. a botched
rotation that reattaches the wrong subtree but stays balanced) would currently
go undetected.

The user asked to upgrade the fuzzer to (1) run at least 100000 random
insert/find/delete operations, (2) call `rb_validate` every 100 operations, and
(3) check operations against a reference model — none of which the current
file fully does. This plan adds a small in-memory shadow/reference model and
cross-checks every operation (and periodically the whole tree) against it,
alongside fixing the validate cadence and the no-arg default iteration count.

Housekeeping agreed with the user: delete the stray `vgcore.3345800` core file
in the repo root before starting (untracked debris from `test_rbtree`); no
investigation of `src/rbtree.c`/`tests/test_rbtree.c` (both already-modified,
unrelated `rb_foreach` work) — out of scope for this task.

## Scope

Single file: `tests/fuzz.c`. Nothing else changes — `include/rbtree.h` is
never touched (graded contract), and the Makefile already passes the right
argv to `fuzz` for `test`/`memcheck`, so it needs no edits.

## Design: shadow reference model

Add a fixed-size array in `main()`:

```c
void *shadow[KEYSPACE] = {0};   /* NULL = key absent from the tree */
```

Sound because `mkkey` (`"k%03d"`) is a bijection between `idx ∈ [0,
KEYSPACE)` and every key string the harness ever generates. For the three
per-op checks below, index directly with the `idx` already computed from the
LCG each iteration — no string parsing needed there. `shadow` never owns or
frees anything; it only stores/overwrites/clears pointers already owned by
`t` (via `rb_create(free)`). Freeing on delete/overwrite/destroy is entirely
the tree's job — the shadow code must never call `free()`.

### Per-operation checks (replacing the current op==0/1/2 branches)

- **Insert** (`op == 0`): after `rb_insert(t, kb, v) == 0` succeeds, set
  `shadow[idx] = v` (bare pointer overwrite — the tree already freed any old
  value via `value_free`). Then immediately assert
  `rb_find(t, kb) == v` to catch a bad insert/rotation at the moment it
  happens rather than waiting for a later random find to land on that key.
- **Find** (`op == 1`): assert `rb_find(t, kb) == shadow[idx]`; on mismatch,
  print iteration, key, expected/actual pointers, and fail.
- **Delete** (`op == 2`): compute `expect_hit = (shadow[idx] != NULL)` before
  calling; assert `(rb_delete(t, kb) == 0) == expect_hit`; then unconditionally
  set `shadow[idx] = NULL` (idempotent on a miss).

### Full-tree cross-check via `rb_foreach`

Add a context struct and callback above `main()`:

```c
typedef struct {
    void * const *shadow;
    int visited[KEYSPACE];
    size_t count;
    int ok;
    char bad_key[16];
    void *bad_expected, *bad_actual;
} cross_check_ctx_t;

static void cross_check_visit(const char *key, void *value, void *ctx) {
    /* parses the numeric suffix back out of "k%03d" via atoi(key+1) — always
     * base-10 (unlike sscanf "%i", which would misread a leading zero as
     * octal), and always round-trips since mkkey/idx is a bijection */
    ...
}

static int cross_check(const rbtree_t *t, void * const shadow[KEYSPACE], long i) {
    /* rb_foreach walk: every visited (key,value) must match shadow[idx];
     * then a second pass over shadow[] confirms no non-NULL entry was left
     * unvisited; finally assert visited count == rb_size(t) == count of
     * non-NULL shadow entries. Prints details and returns -1 on any mismatch. */
    ...
}
```

This directly satisfies "check against a reference model": every visited
node matches the shadow, nothing in the shadow is missing from the tree, and
the counts agree three ways (foreach walk, `rb_size`, shadow scan).

### Wiring into `main()`

- Change the no-arg default: `long iters = (argc > 1) ? strtol(argv[1], NULL, 10) : 100000;`
  (keeps the CLI override so `make memcheck`'s `20000` is unaffected).
- Change the validate cadence from `if (i % 50 == 0)` to
  `if ((i + 1) % 100 == 0)` — fires after operations #100, #200, ... (the
  literal reading of "every 100 operations"; `i % 100 == 0` would instead
  fire after op #1 then #101, #201, ...). Inside that block, call both
  `rb_validate(t)` and the new `cross_check(t, shadow, i)`.
- After the main loop, keep the unconditional final `rb_validate` and add an
  unconditional final `cross_check` right after it, so a tail of <100
  leftover operations still gets one last full check regardless of `iters`.
- Leave the trailing 1000-cycle plain `rb_create(NULL)`/`rb_destroy` pass
  untouched (unrelated allocation-path coverage).
- Add a small `static int fail(rbtree_t *t, const char *fmt, ...)` helper
  (using `<stdarg.h>`) that prints to stderr, destroys `t`, and returns
  `EXIT_FAILURE` — the number of distinct failure sites grows from 3 to ~7
  with this change, so this avoids repeating the same three lines everywhere
  while keeping error messages consistent (iteration number + context on
  every failure).

### Watch-list while implementing

- `atoi`, not `sscanf("%i", ...)`, for parsing the key suffix (avoid the
  octal-leading-zero gotcha).
- `cross_check_ctx_t` must be freshly zero-initialized (`= {0}`) on every
  call — it's called up to ~1000 times over a 100000-iteration run.
- `void *shadow[KEYSPACE]` and `int visited[KEYSPACE]` are fixed-size arrays
  off a `#define` constant, not VLAs.
- Keep every non-obvious loop's one-line invariant comment (CLAUDE.md style
  rule) — the shadow-scan loop and the `rb_foreach` callback both need one.
- `-Wall -Wextra -Werror`: the `rb_foreach` callback uses all three
  parameters (key, value, ctx), so no unused-parameter cast needed.
- Preserve the existing ownership handling for insert failure (`rb_insert`
  returning -1 on OOM: `free(v)` before failing, since the tree never
  consumed it) — unchanged from the current code.

## Verification

1. `git rm`-free delete of `vgcore.3345800` (it's untracked, so a plain `rm`
   plus confirming `git status` no longer lists it).
2. `make test` — must build both binaries and have `test_rbtree` and the
   upgraded `fuzz 100000` both pass, with periodic and final validate +
   cross-check succeeding.
3. `make asan` — rebuild with ASan/UBSan, rerun `make test` clean.
4. `make memcheck` — valgrind clean (no leaks, no errors) on both binaries,
   `fuzz` run with `20000` iterations.
5. Manually run `./build/fuzz` with no args and confirm it prints a final
   summary reflecting 100000 ops (new default) with no failures.
6. Confirm existing `tests/test_rbtree.c` and `src/rbtree.c` are left
   byte-for-byte unmodified by this change (`git diff --stat` shows only
   `tests/fuzz.c`).

- `atoi`, not `sscanf("%i", ...)`, for parsing the key suffix (avoid the
  octal-leading-zero gotcha).
- `cross_check_ctx_t` must be freshly zero-initialized (`= {0}`) on every
  call — it's called up to ~1000 times over a 100000-iteration run.
- `void *shadow[KEYSPACE]` and `int visited[KEYSPACE]` are fixed-size arrays
  off a `#define` constant, not VLAs.
- Keep every non-obvious loop's one-line invariant comment (CLAUDE.md style
  rule) — the shadow-scan loop and the `rb_foreach` callback both need one.
- `-Wall -Wextra -Werror`: the `rb_foreach` callback uses all three
  parameters (key, value, ctx), so no unused-parameter cast needed.
- Preserve the existing ownership handling for insert failure (`rb_insert`
  returning -1 on OOM: `free(v)` before failing, since the tree never
  consumed it) — unchanged from the current code.

## Verification

1. `git rm`-free delete of `vgcore.3345800` (it's untracked, so a plain `rm`
   plus confirming `git status` no longer lists it).
2. `make test` — must build both binaries and have `test_rbtree` and the
   upgraded `fuzz 100000` both pass, with periodic and final validate +
   cross-check succeeding.
3. `make asan` — rebuild with ASan/UBSan, rerun `make test` clean.
4. `make memcheck` — valgrind clean (no leaks, no errors) on both binaries,
   `fuzz` run with `20000` iterations.
5. Manually run `./build/fuzz` with no args and confirm it prints a final
   summary reflecting 100000 ops (new default) with no failures.
6. Confirm existing `tests/test_rbtree.c` and `src/rbtree.c` are left
   byte-for-byte unmodified by this change (`git diff --stat` shows only
   `tests/fuzz.c`).

entries.name: ExitPlanMode
entries.description:
Use this tool when you are in plan mode and have finished writing your plan to the plan file and are ready for user approval.

## How This Tool Works
- You should have already written your plan to the plan file specified in the plan mode system message
- This tool does NOT take the plan content as a parameter - it will read the plan from the file you wrote
- This tool simply signals that you're done planning and ready for the user to review and approve
- The user will see the contents of your plan file when they review it

## When to Use This Tool
IMPORTANT: Only use this tool when the task requires planning the implementation steps of a task that requires writing code. For research tasks where you're gathering information, searching files, reading files or in general trying to understand the codebase - do NOT use this tool.

## Before Using This Tool
Ensure your plan is complete and unambiguous:
- If you have unresolved questions about requirements or approach, use AskUserQuestion first (in earlier phases)
- Once your plan is finalized, use THIS tool to request approval

**Important:** Do NOT use AskUserQuestion to ask "Is this plan okay?" or "Should I proceed?" - that's exactly what THIS tool does. ExitPlanMode inherently requests user approval of your plan.

## Examples

1. Initial task: "Search for and understand the implementation of vim mode in the codebase" - Do not use the exit plan mode tool because you are not planning the implementation steps of a task.
2. Initial task: "Help me implement yank mode for vim" - Use the exit plan mode tool after you have finished planning the implementation steps of the task.
3. Initial task: "Add a new feature to handle user authentication" - If unsure about auth method (OAuth, JWT, etc.), use AskUserQuestion first, then use exit plan mode tool after clarifying the approach.

content.text:
All three required checks pass clean:

- **`make test`** — `test_rbtree` and `fuzz` (100000 ops, default) both pass.
- **`make asan`** — clean rebuild under ASan/UBSan, `make test` passes.
- **`make memcheck`** — valgrind clean on both binaries (0 leaks, 0 errors), `fuzz` run at 20000 ops.

Changes to `tests/fuzz.c`:
- Added a `shadow[KEYSPACE]` reference model mirroring exactly which keys are present in the tree and which pointer each holds. Every insert, find, and delete is cross-checked against it (insert also does an immediate post-insert `rb_find` self-check).
- Added a `cross_check()` helper that walks the real tree via `rb_foreach` and verifies it against `shadow[]` node-by-node, confirming no entries are missing/extra and that counts agree three ways (`rb_foreach` visits, `rb_size`, shadow count).
- Validate cadence changed from every 50 to exactly every 100 operations (`(i+1) % 100 == 0`), pairing `rb_validate` with the new `cross_check` each time, plus a final pass after the loop.
- Default iteration count (no CLI arg) bumped from 1000 to 100000, so the binary alone satisfies "at least 100000 operations" regardless of how it's invoked.
- Added a small `fail()` helper to keep the now-larger set of failure sites consistent (destroys the tree, reports iteration + context, returns `EXIT_FAILURE`).

Also incidentally explained the mystery `vgcore.3345800` you had in the repo root: `make asan` leaves ASan-instrumented binaries in `build/`, and running `make memcheck` afterward without a `make clean` in between hands valgrind an ASan binary, which segfaults immediately (a known ASan/valgrind incompatibility, not a bug in your tree). I hit and cleaned up a fresh instance of the same thing during verification — worth remembering to `make clean` between `asan` and `memcheck` runs.
